article: Solar power capacity grew faster last year than in any previous year, according to an industry report. Installations rose by more than a third as panel prices fell and governments offered tax credits. China accounted for roughly half of all new capacity, while India and Brazil also set records. Analysts say the rapid growth is changing electricity markets, pushing wholesale prices down at midday when solar output peaks. Grid operators are now racing to add batteries so that cheap daytime power can be used in the evening. The report warns that transmission bottlenecks and slow permitting could limit growth unless regulators act quickly.
reference: Solar capacity grew faster than ever last year, led by China, as falling prices and tax credits drove installations, though grid bottlenecks and slow permitting could limit further growth.

article: A two-year study of 4,000 employees found that hybrid work schedules improved retention without hurting productivity. Workers who spent two days at home each week were 33 percent less likely to quit than colleagues who were in the office full time. Managers rated performance and promotion rates as essentially unchanged between the groups. The researchers noted that the benefits were largest for employees with long commutes and young children. However, they cautioned that new hires may miss out on mentoring when teams are rarely in the same room. Companies are advised to coordinate office days so that collaboration time is not lost.
reference: A two-year study found hybrid work cut quit rates by a third with no productivity loss, but researchers warn new hires may lose mentoring if office days are not coordinated.

article: Marine biologists have begun planting lab-grown coral fragments on damaged reefs in the Indian Ocean. The fragments are raised in nurseries from corals that survived recent heat waves, in the hope that they will tolerate warmer water. Early monitoring shows survival rates above 70 percent after eighteen months. Local fishing communities help with the planting and earn income from guiding visitors to the restored sites. Scientists stress that restoration cannot replace cutting carbon emissions, because repeated bleaching events would still destroy young colonies. They say the projects mainly buy time for reefs while the climate stabilises.
reference: Scientists are replanting heat-tolerant lab-grown coral on Indian Ocean reefs with over 70 percent survival, but stress that cutting emissions is still essential to protect them.

article: Electric vehicle sales in India doubled this year, driven mainly by two-wheelers and three-wheeled taxis. Government subsidies and lower running costs have made electric scooters attractive to city commuters. Cars remain a small share of the market because of high prices and limited public charging. Manufacturers have announced new factories for batteries and motors, promising thousands of jobs. Experts say that a reliable charging network and cheaper financing will decide whether electric cars follow the same path. Cities are also adding electric buses, which have cut fuel costs for public transport operators.
reference: Indian electric vehicle sales doubled, led by scooters and taxis, but cars lag behind because of high prices and sparse charging, so charging networks and financing will be key.

article: New research suggests that deep sleep plays a central role in turning daily experiences into lasting memories. In experiments, volunteers who learned a set of word pairs and then slept performed far better the next day than those who stayed awake. Brain recordings showed bursts of activity called sleep spindles replaying the new material. When researchers gently disrupted these bursts, memory scores dropped sharply. The team says the findings could help explain why chronic sleep loss harms learning in students. They recommend consistent bedtimes and avoiding screens late at night to protect deep sleep.
reference: Research shows deep sleep, especially sleep spindles, helps consolidate memories, so disrupting it hurts learning and consistent bedtimes are recommended.

article: Several large cities are expanding their metro networks to cut traffic and air pollution. New lines are planned to connect suburbs with business districts, and fares will be integrated across buses and trains. Planners say that every kilometre of metro line removes thousands of car trips each day. Construction is expensive and often delayed by land acquisition and utility relocation. Residents worry about noise and temporary road closures during the building phase. City officials argue that the long-term benefits for commuting times and air quality outweigh the short-term disruption.
reference: Large cities are expanding metro networks with integrated fares to reduce traffic and pollution, accepting costs and construction disruption for long-term benefits.
